**U.S. Health Insurance, Explained via Fantasy Football**

Imagine the entire U.S. healthcare system is one massive, 32-team fantasy football league that somehow got turned into a for-profit religion. You are not the owner. You are a bench player who never gets to touch the ball but is still somehow financially responsible for the whole damn franchise.

### The Draft (Enrollment)

Every year you have to “draft” your insurance during Open Enrollment, which is like fantasy football’s waiver wire but the only players available are three overpriced tight ends, a defense that’s already on IR, and one guy who used to be good in 2017. You stare at the options for six hours, compare obscure stats no one understands (deductible, out-of-pocket maximum, coinsurance, network), and ultimately pick the team that looks least likely to bankrupt you if your star running back (your pancreas) suddenly ruptures.

You draft a Bronze plan. It’s the fantasy equivalent of drafting a kicker in round one because it was the only thing left and your league has weird rules.

### The Roster (Your Plan)

Your Bronze plan is basically a roster full of practice-squad guys. They’re “in-network,” which means they theoretically play for your franchise, but they almost never see the field unless you first get crushed by the Injury Reserve (a $2,000 deductible).

Every time you want to see a doctor, it’s like trying to start a player who’s on bye. The front office (insurance company) says, “Sorry, that specialist is only available in weeks 14–17 and only if you’ve already lost three games by 17 points.” That’s your referral process.

### The Weekly Matchup (Getting Sick)

You wake up with strep throat. This is now a fantasy football emergency. You go to urgent care, which is the equivalent of starting a random handcuff off waivers because your RB1 twisted an ankle at practice.

The urgent care bills you $180 after insurance. It’s just how the league works.
